title: Complex eyes can be built by selection through graded useful steps

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Complex eyes can be built by selection through graded useful steps

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Natural selection could have converted a simple optic nerve coated with pigment and covered by transparent membrane into a highly perfect eye through a series of graded steps, each useful to its possessor, as shown by the graduated diversity of eyes in living crustaceans.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I can see no very great difficulty (not more than in the case of many other structures) in believing that natural selection has converted the simple apparatus of an optic nerve merely coated with pigment and invested by transparent membrane, into an optical instrument as perfect as is possessed by any member of the great Articulate class.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VI, “Difficulties on Theory”; section “Organs of extreme perfection.”. Scope: eyes of Articulata (arthropods and allies), extended to vertebrates

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch06-07: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.60

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Comparative morphology and phylogenies can test graded transitions and functional plausibility. They cannot directly observe the complete historical path or uniquely attribute it to natural selection.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Map eye complexity, optical performance, ecology, and phylogeny across arthropods, then test whether inferred transitions are mostly small and whether intermediate states improve performance. A well-supported phylogenetic sequence lacking viable intermediates would count against the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Living forms are not literal ancestors.

Fitness effects of historical intermediate eyes are usually unmeasured.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.55
discriminating power: 0.48
data adequacy: 0.55
data existence: 0.72
operationalizability: 0.68

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The comparative series Darwin appealed to can be approximated with phylogeny plus morphology, but eye-grade and optical-performance variables are not in one open table, so a team would spend months compiling them. Even a clean series would not reconstruct the historical path or separate selection from shared developmental constraint. Coverage is decent for insects and crustaceans and thin for the vertebrate extension of the scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Score optical complexity (pigment, lens, aperture, resolution) across arthropods on an independent phylogeny and ask whether neighboring grades are each optically functional. A continuous series of useful grades would support the possibility of a selective path; a complex eye isolated from any functional intermediate, or intermediates that are optically useless, would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Living grades are collateral relatives, not the ancestral sequence.

No public dataset scores optical performance across Articulata; those measurements are scattered in papers.

A functional series shows that intermediates are possible, not that selection produced any particular eye.
